A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs describe the same UFT research, authors, methods, and mathematical reasoning benchmarks. The complete 21-page v1 and 23-page v3, including appendices A–D, provide readable text, equations, tables, and figures that support reliable matching.

before.justification: Tables 1–3 and Appendix C report original Qwen2.5-Math fine-tuning experiments, including success rates, inference times, and learning-rate and unlikelihood-loss analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains the original fine-tuning experiments and adds empirical SimPO and CPO-SimPO comparisons, training-data analyses, and preliminary resource measurements.

M1.justification: The proposed reasoning-data generation, unpaired positive/negative training batches, combined NLL and unlikelihood objective, and inference procedures remain unchanged in Algorithm 1 and Equations 1–6. The added preference objectives describe comparison methods rather than changes to UFT.

E1.justification: Both versions use Countdown and Game-of-24, including Countdown-to-Game-of-24 transfer and the same target-number and difficulty-based generalization scenarios. Preliminary Mistral 7B experiments also appear in both. No new dataset, domain, or task requirement is introduced.

E2.justification: v3 adds SimPO and CPO-SimPO to the comparisons in Tables 2–3, and CPO-SimPO to Table 1. These substantially extend v1's SFT and inference-time comparisons to competing methods that use negative data. CPO-SimPO is distinct from the Chain of Preference Optimization work merely cited in v1.

E3.justification: The added preference comparisons introduce filtering for inputs with both successful and failed paths, E sampled preference pairs per successful path, and fixed baseline parameters beta=0.1, gamma=0.5, and lambda=1.0 (Appendix A.2). Existing UFT/SFT splits, model sizes, epochs, evaluation sampling, and learning-rate sweeps are retained.

E4.justification: The SimPO versus CPO-SimPO comparison adds a targeted examination of the NLL term, while new Table 5 quantifies correct paths excluded by preference pairing. Existing learning-rate, data-source, and unlikelihood-weight analyses remain; merging v1 Figures 6–7 into v3 Figure 6 does not remove those analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report three fine-tuning seeds for Countdown and four for Game-of-24, with the same plus/minus entries and shaded uncertainty displays. The added comparator results follow this existing practice; no new statistical test, uncertainty definition, or estimation procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: v3 adds complete preference-baseline result grids. For example, Table 2 reports 7B Countdown mixed-data greedy accuracy of 0.0% for SimPO and 50.6% for CPO-SimPO, alongside retained SFT 55.4% and UFT 57.4%. All 72 matched SFT/UFT mean-and-uncertainty entries in Tables 2–3 are unchanged. New training-cost findings are added, while v1 Table 5's fine-tuned 1.5B inference-time entries are omitted.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds Equations 7–9 defining SimPO, CPO-SimPO, and non-iterative RPO objectives, together with conditions relating the latter two mathematically. The MDP formulation, UFT objectives, gradients, and shared-prefix reasoning remain unchanged; no new UFT theorem or proof is supplied.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction expand the comparative claims to superiority over preference-based learning and greater reliability of unpaired forgetting, beyond v1's emphasis on SFT and inference-time search. The claimed average forgetting gain narrows from 1–3% to 1–2%, while the data-quality, small-learning-rate, and 180-fold inference-cost claims remain.

C2.justification: v3 interprets SimPO's poor results as evidence that NLL is essential, and hypothesizes that pairing-induced data loss and objective balancing explain CPO-SimPO's contrasting Countdown/Game-of-24 behavior. Appendix D also explicitly limits small-learning-rate benefits on Mistral and suggests that applicability depends more on base reasoning ability than model size.

D1.justification: v3 adds a dedicated project-code access link, explicitly states full-parameter fine-tuning, and documents TRL baseline implementations, pairing construction, and loss parameters in Appendix A. Appendix B and Table 5 expand dataset counts and comparative training-cost information. The v1 statement that each failed path is seen only once is omitted.

R1.justification: Research positioning expands around paired versus unpaired data and reference-model requirements, including SimPO, CPO, KTO, and the new Table 4 taxonomy. v3 develops the connection to RPO and replaces v1's assertion that the learning-rate finding is novel with connections to loss-landscape and preference-optimization research.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled, with substantial revisions to the abstract, motivation, negative-data related work, and results interpretation around unpaired offline learning. The appendices are reorganized from Reasoner Details/Fine-tuning Details/Additional Results to Fine-tuning Details/Additional Results/Reasoner Details, with more explicit subsection structure.

P2.justification: Tables 1–3 are substantially redesigned with method columns, explicit training regimes, and color highlighting. Figure 1 adds CPO-SimPO and revises the displayed SFT comparison; new method-comparison and dataset-statistics tables are introduced. Appendix figures are relocated and merged, and typography, headers, margins, and captions are revised throughout.

improvement.justification: v3 improves comparative validation through relevant preference baselines, clearer training-regime comparisons, and substantially better implementation and data documentation. These gains are tempered by omitted 1.5B timing details and an overly broad abstract claim of consistent superiority: Table 3 reports CPO-SimPO at 27.5% versus UFT at 23.2% for 7B CoT-data pass@1. The paper is easier to assess and reproduce, although its strongest new claims require qualification.
